questions.stem: Hammurabi, who ruled Babylon from about 1792 to 1750 BCE, belonged to which people?
options: The Elamites
The Amorites
The Kassites
The Hittites
questions.explanation: Hammurabi was an Amorite, from a semi-nomadic people who moved into Mesopotamia late in the third millennium and founded dynasties in several cities. The Kassites ruled Babylon after the Hittite sack of 1595 BCE.

questions.stem: Early in his reign Hammurabi ruled only a modest kingdom around Babylon. By the end he controlled most of Mesopotamia because he:
options: was given the land by the Hittite king as a reward for loyalty
used alliances and then war to defeat rivals such as Larsa and Mari
inherited the whole of Mesopotamia from his father as a single kingdom
was invited by the Sumerian assembly to rule all of its cities
questions.explanation: Hammurabi spent years in shifting alliances, including with Zimri-Lim of Mari, before turning on his rivals, conquering Rim-Sin of Larsa and then Mari itself. His father left him a small kingdom, not an empire.

questions.stem: Under the First Babylonian Dynasty, the god Marduk became more important because:
options: he was the patron god of Ur, which the Babylonians wished to honour
Sargon of Akkad had named Marduk the chief god of his whole empire
he was the patron god of Babylon, which had become the centre of power
the Hittites made the worship of Marduk compulsory in all of their lands
questions.explanation: As Babylon rose to dominate Mesopotamia, its city god Marduk rose with it, eventually becoming head of the Babylonian pantheon. The patron god of Ur was the moon god Nanna.

questions.stem: Which change best shows how the expression of power changed under Hammurabi compared with the earlier city-states of Sumer?
options: One king ruled many cities from Babylon and issued laws for all his lands
Each city was ruled again by its own priest-king in the name of its god
Kings stopped claiming any link with the gods and ruled only by armed force
Power passed from kings to assemblies of elders elected in each city
questions.explanation: Hammurabi governed a territorial kingdom from Babylon and presented himself as the king who brought justice to the whole land, chosen by the gods. Separate city-states under their own rulers describe the earlier Sumerian pattern, and kings still claimed divine support.

questions.stem: The best-known copy of the Laws of Hammurabi is carved on a stone stele that was found in 1901 at:
options: Nineveh, among the tablets of Ashurbanipal's library
Mari, buried in the ruins of the palace of Zimri-Lim
Susa, in Elam, where it had been carried as war booty
Babylon, standing in the main temple of the god Marduk
questions.explanation: The stele was taken from Babylonia to Susa by an Elamite king in the twelfth century BCE, which is where French archaeologists found it. It is now in the Louvre in Paris.

questions.stem: In the prologue to his laws, Hammurabi says that the gods called him to rule so that:
options: every man would own an equal field
the strong might not oppress the weak
the gods would be fed by the people
Babylon would conquer the whole world
questions.explanation: The prologue presents Hammurabi as chosen by the gods to bring justice to the land and protect the weak. This presents the king as a just shepherd of his people, an important part of how he expressed his power.

questions.stem: One law of Hammurabi states that if a man destroys the eye of another man of the awilum class, his own eye is to be destroyed. This is an example of:
options: a punishment that applied equally to every class of person
lex talionis, the principle of punishment matching the injury
trial by ordeal, in which the gods decided guilt or innocence
a fine in silver, the usual penalty for any injury in Babylon
questions.explanation: Lex talionis, ‘an eye for an eye’, matches the punishment to the harm done. In the laws it applies between members of the awilum class; injuring a commoner or a slave was punished by payment in silver instead.

questions.stem: Under the Laws of Hammurabi, destroying the eye of an awilum cost the offender his own eye, destroying the eye of a mushkenum cost a mina of silver, and destroying a slave's eye cost half the slave's value. What does this best show?
options: Babylonian courts punished every injury with a fine paid in silver
Slaves were treated as equal to free people under Babylonian law
The laws were mainly concerned with protecting the temple's wealth
Babylonian society was divided into classes with unequal legal protection
questions.explanation: The different penalties show three legal classes: awilum (free persons of higher status), mushkenum (commoners or dependants) and wardum (slaves). The law gave the greatest protection to the highest class. Only some injuries were punished by fines.

questions.stem: A law of Hammurabi says that if a builder builds a house badly and it collapses and kills the owner, the builder is to be put to death. This law shows that Babylonian law:
options: held craftsmen responsible for the safety of their work
protected builders from claims by the families of owners
left the punishment of builders to the priests of Marduk
applied only to buildings that belonged to the king
questions.explanation: The law makes the builder answerable with his own life for a fatal collapse, showing a concern with professional responsibility. A related law punishes the builder's son if the owner's son is killed, another example of matching penalties.

questions.stem: In the epilogue, Hammurabi invites any wronged man to come before his statue and have the stele read to him. A historian could best use this to argue that the laws were intended to:
options: be read privately by scribes and kept hidden from ordinary people
show that Hammurabi had no need to claim the support of the gods
display the king as a just ruler to his people and to the gods
replace all earlier laws of Sumer and Akkad, which were forgotten
questions.explanation: Setting up the stele in public and inviting the wronged to consult it advertised Hammurabi as the guardian of justice. Historians debate how far courts actually applied the laws, and the code drew on older Mesopotamian traditions rather than replacing them.

questions.stem: Historians often doubt that the Laws of Hammurabi were a complete legal code applied in every court. Which evidence best supports this doubt?
options: Surviving court records from the period rarely refer to the laws
The laws were carved in stone rather than written on clay tablets
The laws were written in Akkadian rather than in Sumerian
The stele shows the king standing before a god at the top
questions.explanation: Thousands of contracts and court records survive from the Old Babylonian period, but they seldom cite the laws, which suggests the stele expressed royal ideals of justice as much as working law. Carving, language and the relief do not bear on how the laws were used.

questions.stem: Shamshi-Adad I, an Amorite ruler of northern Mesopotamia, placed his son Yasmah-Addu on the throne of:
options: Uruk
Mari
Babylon
Larsa
questions.explanation: Shamshi-Adad built a large kingdom in northern Mesopotamia, ruling it with his sons: Yasmah-Addu at Mari and Ishme-Dagan at Ekallatum. After Shamshi-Adad's death, Zimri-Lim regained the throne of Mari.

questions.stem: In letters found at Mari, Shamshi-Adad scolds Yasmah-Addu and compares him with his brother, who is winning victories. These letters are most useful as evidence of:
options: the exact size of the armies that fought at the battle for Babylon
the private thoughts of the ordinary farmers who lived in the kingdom of Mari
the laws that Shamshi-Adad issued for every city in Mesopotamia
how a king managed his kingdom through his sons and judged their rule
questions.explanation: The letters show Shamshi-Adad directing his sons, criticising Yasmah-Addu as weak and praising Ishme-Dagan's successes, so they reveal how power was shared and supervised within the royal family. They are royal correspondence, not legal texts or the views of farmers.

questions.stem: Shamshi-Adad's letters to Yasmah-Addu are highly critical. Which limitation should a historian keep in mind when using them to judge Yasmah-Addu's rule?
options: They give only the father's view, and not all of the son's replies survive
They were written centuries after both men had died, by Babylonian scribes
They were translated into Greek and changed by later copyists over time
They were carved on public monuments meant to be read by the citizens of Mari
questions.explanation: The letters show a demanding father's perspective, which may exaggerate his son's failings, and we cannot always read the other side of the exchange. They are original tablets written during the men's lives, not later copies or public inscriptions.

questions.stem: The archaeologist who excavated Mari from 1933 and uncovered the palace of Zimri-Lim was:
options: Austen Henry Layard
André Parrot
Leonard Woolley
Hormuzd Rassam
questions.explanation: André Parrot led the French excavations at Mari after a local discovery of a statue in 1933. Woolley excavated Ur, while Layard and Rassam worked at the Assyrian sites of Nimrud and Nineveh.

questions.stem: Thousands of cuneiform tablets were found in the palace of Zimri-Lim at Mari. Most of them are:
options: copies of the Epic of Gilgamesh and other long poems
law codes carved by order of the kings of Babylon
astronomical diaries recording the movements of planets
letters and administrative records of the royal palace
questions.explanation: The Mari archives are mainly royal letters, accounts and economic texts, which show diplomacy, trade, prophecy and daily administration in the Old Babylonian period. Astronomical diaries come much later, from the first millennium BCE.

questions.stem: Why is the Mari archive so valuable for understanding the First Babylonian Dynasty, even though Mari was not part of Babylon?
options: Its letters record diplomacy with Hammurabi and other kings from Mari's viewpoint
It contains the only surviving copy of the Laws of Hammurabi on clay tablets
Its tablets were written by Hammurabi himself while he lived in the palace of Mari
It proves that Mari had been the capital of Babylonia before Hammurabi moved it
questions.explanation: Mari's correspondents reported on the alliances, wars and messengers of rival kings, including Hammurabi, so the archive gives a contemporary view of Babylon's rise from outside. Hammurabi later conquered Mari, which ends the archive.

questions.stem: The palace archive at Mari ends about 1761 BCE because:
options: Shamshi-Adad moved the royal archive to his capital at Ashur
Hammurabi conquered Mari and later destroyed its walls and palace
the Euphrates changed its course and the city's people moved away upstream
the Hittites sacked Mari on their way to attack Babylon
questions.explanation: After years as Zimri-Lim's ally, Hammurabi conquered Mari and then destroyed it. The fire and abandonment that followed preserved the tablets in the ruins. The Hittite raid on Babylon came more than 150 years later.

questions.stem: The First Babylonian Dynasty ended in 1595 BCE when Babylon was sacked by:
options: the Assyrians under Sennacherib
the Elamites under Shutruk-Nakhunte
the Medes under Cyaxares
the Hittites under Mursili I
questions.explanation: The Hittite king Mursili I raided Babylon in 1595 BCE (by the commonly used chronology) and ended the dynasty. Sennacherib destroyed Babylon about 900 years later, and the Medes helped bring down Assyria.

questions.stem: Which group filled the power vacuum in Babylonia after the Hittite sack and ruled there for about four centuries?
options: The Persians
The Kassites
The Amorites
The Sumerians
questions.explanation: The Hittites withdrew after their raid, and the Kassites took control of Babylon, ruling for roughly four hundred years. The Amorite dynasty was the one that had just fallen.

questions.stem: Babylon's power weakened under Hammurabi's son Samsu-iluna, who faced revolts and lost control of the far south. What does this suggest about Hammurabi's empire?
options: It was so well organised that it could not be challenged after his death
It was already ruled by the Kassites in the last years of Hammurabi's life
It had always been a loose alliance with no king at its head in Babylon
It depended heavily on one ruler's personal authority and military success
questions.explanation: Rapid conquests under Hammurabi were not matched by lasting loyalty, so revolts broke out once he died. This pattern of a strong founder followed by fragmentation recurs in Mesopotamian history. The Kassites took over only after 1595 BCE.

questions.stem: The Assyrian Empire took its name from the city of Ashur and from:
options: its main river, the Ashur
its mountain range, the Ashur
its chief god, Ashur
its first king, Ashur
questions.explanation: Ashur was both the city on the Tigris and the god who was its patron; Assyrian kings ruled as the god's representatives and fought wars in his name. The river at Ashur is the Tigris.

questions.stem: Assurnasirpal II (883–859 BCE) moved the capital of Assyria from Ashur to:
options: Babylon
Dur-Sharrukin (Khorsabad)
Kalhu (Nimrud)
Nineveh
questions.explanation: Assurnasirpal II rebuilt Kalhu, now Nimrud, with the Northwest Palace as his new capital. Sargon II later built Dur-Sharrukin, and Sennacherib made Nineveh the capital.

questions.stem: Assurnasirpal II's annals boast of flaying rebels and piling up the heads of the defeated. A historian should interpret these accounts mainly as:
options: propaganda meant to terrify enemies and warn subjects against revolt
neutral military records written by enemies who had escaped Assyria
evidence that the Assyrians never offered conquered cities any terms
private letters from the king to his son about how to run the army
questions.explanation: Royal annals were written for the king to glorify his power, and their accounts of terror were meant to deter resistance. They may exaggerate, and other evidence shows cities that submitted were usually spared. They are royal, not enemy, sources.

questions.stem: Assurnasirpal II's Banquet Stele describes a feast for tens of thousands of guests. It was set up to celebrate:
options: the marriage of his daughter to an Egyptian king
the completion of his new capital at Kalhu
his victory over the Hittites at Babylon
the founding of the Royal Library of Nineveh
questions.explanation: The stele records a ten-day feast for the inauguration of Kalhu and its palace, a display of wealth and generosity meant to impress. The library at Nineveh belonged to Ashurbanipal, two centuries later.

questions.stem: Which reform did Tiglath-pileser III introduce?
options: A law that let conquered kingdoms keep their own armies and kings
A single coinage of silver used for all taxes across the empire
A standing professional army that included troops from conquered lands
A council of priests that chose each new king from within the royal family
questions.explanation: Tiglath-pileser III built a permanent army, partly from foreign contingents, instead of relying on seasonal levies. He turned many vassal kingdoms into provinces rather than leaving them their own kings and armies. Coins were not yet in use.

questions.stem: Tiglath-pileser III split the larger provinces into smaller ones, each under a governor he appointed. The main purpose of this reform was to:
options: reduce the number of officials and leave the provinces to govern themselves
allow each governor to keep all the tribute he collected for his own use
stop powerful officials from building up enough strength to challenge the king
give local kings more freedom to rule their lands in their own traditional way
questions.explanation: In the decades before his reign, great Assyrian officials had become powerful enough to act independently. Smaller provinces under royal appointees reduced that risk and tied administration to the king. The reform increased, not reduced, central control.

questions.stem: Mass deportation of conquered peoples to other parts of the empire, used heavily from the reign of Tiglath-pileser III, served mainly to:
options: break local resistance and supply labour and soldiers where needed
return conquered peoples to the lands their ancestors had come from
punish only the kings of conquered lands while sparing their people
give the Assyrian people new homes in the lands they had captured
questions.explanation: Moving whole communities weakened their ties to their homeland, making revolt harder, while giving the empire workers, farmers and troops. Deportees were usually resettled away from home, not returned to ancestral lands.

questions.stem: Which Assyrian king made Nineveh his capital and rebuilt it on a grand scale?
options: Tiglath-pileser III
Shamshi-Adad I
Sennacherib
Assurnasirpal II
questions.explanation: Sennacherib (705–681 BCE) moved the capital to Nineveh and rebuilt it with a great palace, new walls and gates, and canals and aqueducts. Assurnasirpal II's capital was Kalhu.

questions.stem: The relief carvings from Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh, now in the British Museum, show his army's siege of:
options: Lachish, a city of the kingdom of Judah
Babylon, the city of the god Marduk
Susa, the capital of the Elamites
Memphis, the old capital of Egypt
questions.explanation: The Lachish reliefs show the siege and capture of Lachish in Judah in 701 BCE, with siege ramps, battering rams and deported families. Sennacherib chose to display this victory prominently in his palace.

questions.stem: Sennacherib's annals say he shut up Hezekiah of Judah in Jerusalem ‘like a bird in a cage’ and took many of his towns. What do the annals not claim?
options: That Hezekiah sent heavy tribute to Sennacherib
That many walled towns of Judah were captured
That Sennacherib captured the city of Jerusalem
That Sennacherib besieged Hezekiah in Jerusalem
questions.explanation: The annals record the capture of many towns, the blockade of Jerusalem and Hezekiah's tribute, but not the capture of Jerusalem itself. Historians note that an Assyrian king would have boasted of such a victory, so the silence is significant.

questions.stem: Sennacherib called his new palace at Nineveh the:
options: ‘Gate of the Gods’
‘Temple of Heaven’
‘Palace Without Rival’
‘House of the Tablets’
questions.explanation: Sennacherib named his Southwest Palace the ‘Palace Without Rival’ and lined its rooms with carved reliefs. The name expressed his claim to unmatched power. ‘Gate of the gods’ is the meaning usually given to the name Babylon.

questions.stem: Sennacherib built canals and the stone aqueduct at Jerwan to bring water to Nineveh. Their main purpose was to:
options: water the city's orchards, gardens and fields from the hills
carry the river trade of the Euphrates past the city walls
drain the marshes so the city could be built on dry land
flood the plain around the city to stop enemy chariots
questions.explanation: The canals and aqueduct carried water from the hills to Nineveh's gardens, parks and fields, showing royal power over nature as well as meeting practical needs. Nineveh is on the Tigris, not the Euphrates.

questions.stem: Nineveh had important temples to Ishtar and to Nabu. Nabu was the god of:
options: the sun and justice
writing and the scribes
war and the hunt
the sea and storms
questions.explanation: Nabu, son of Marduk, was the god of writing and wisdom, patron of scribes. Ishtar, the goddess of love and war, was the great goddess of Nineveh. The sun god of justice was Shamash.

questions.stem: The Royal Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh is especially significant to historians because it:
options: preserved thousands of tablets including the fullest version of Gilgamesh
contained the original stele of the Laws of Hammurabi from Babylon
held the only Mesopotamian texts written on papyrus scrolls
was the first library anywhere in which tablets were written in Sumerian
questions.explanation: Ashurbanipal collected literary, religious, medical and omen texts from across Mesopotamia. Its tablets, excavated in the 1850s, include the Standard Babylonian version of Gilgamesh. The Hammurabi stele was found at Susa.

questions.stem: A relief from Ashurbanipal's palace shows the king and queen feasting in a garden while the head of a defeated Elamite king hangs from a nearby tree. What message was the relief most likely meant to convey?
options: Ashurbanipal preferred life in his gardens to leading the army in war
The Elamite king had been invited to Nineveh as an honoured guest
Assyrian queens ruled the empire while the king was away at war
Peace and plenty for Assyria rest on the king's victory over his enemies
questions.explanation: The calm garden and the enemy's head together present Assyrian prosperity as the reward of royal victory. Palace reliefs were carefully designed propaganda for visitors and officials. Nothing in the scene suggests the queen ruled.

questions.stem: Nineveh fell in 612 BCE to an alliance of:
options: the Hittites and the Kassites
the Egyptians and the Elamites
the Persians and the Greeks
the Babylonians and the Medes
questions.explanation: Babylonians under Nabopolassar and Medes under Cyaxares captured and sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE. Egypt was in fact an ally of the last Assyrian kings, and the Hittite kingdom had long gone.

questions.stem: Which cause most weakened Assyria before the attack on Nineveh?
options: Civil wars between rival claimants to the throne after Ashurbanipal's reign
The Hittite sack of Babylon, which cut Assyria off from its southern trade
The loss of its standing army after the death of Tiglath-pileser III
A long drought that forced the court to abandon Nineveh for Babylon
questions.explanation: After Ashurbanipal, rival kings and generals fought over the throne while Babylon broke away under Nabopolassar. Former vassals took advantage of the turmoil. The Hittite sack was almost a thousand years earlier.

questions.stem: Historians debate how and why Nineveh was destroyed. Which statement is the most defensible?
options: The Assyrians themselves destroyed Nineveh to stop the Babylonians from using it
Burnt layers and bodies at the gates show a violent assault, though details are unclear
Babylonian texts prove that a Tigris flood on its own destroyed the walls of Nineveh
The city was abandoned peacefully when the Assyrian king handed it to the Medes
questions.explanation: Excavations show burning and unburied bodies at gates such as the Halzi Gate, and the Babylonian chronicle records the city's capture. Later Greek stories of a flood are not confirmed, so the exact course of the attack remains debated.

questions.stem: We divide an hour into 60 minutes and a circle into 360 degrees. This comes from the Mesopotamian:
options: base-12 (duodecimal) number system
base-2 (binary) counting system
base-60 (sexagesimal) number system
base-10 (decimal) number system
questions.explanation: Mesopotamian mathematicians counted in base 60, which divides easily into many factors. Their use of it in astronomy and time measurement passed down to us in hours, minutes and degrees.

questions.stem: The Babylonian calendar was based on the moon. To keep it in step with the seasons, priests:
options: removed five days from every month
started each year on a different day
counted only the hours of daylight
added an extra month in some years
questions.explanation: Twelve lunar months fall about 11 days short of a solar year, so an intercalary month was added when needed to keep festivals and farming in line with the seasons.

questions.stem: Mesopotamian scholars watched the sky closely, and omen series such as Enuma Anu Enlil linked celestial events to the fate of the king. This shows that astronomy was valued mainly because it:
options: proved that the earth moved around the sun each year
was taught to every child as part of village schooling
helped interpret the will of the gods for the king and the state
allowed sailors to find their way across the Mediterranean Sea
questions.explanation: Observations of eclipses, planets and the moon were recorded as signs from the gods, so astronomy served divination for the king. The systematic records it produced later fed into precise astronomy. Mesopotamians did not hold a sun-centred model.

questions.stem: Mesopotamian medicine had two kinds of healer. The ashipu mainly:
options: set broken bones and applied bandages and plasters made from herbs
trained scribes to read the omens written in the stars each night
pulled teeth and made false ones from ivory and gold for the elite
diagnosed illness as the work of gods or spirits and used incantations
questions.explanation: The ashipu treated illness as a sign of divine or demonic action and used rituals and incantations, while the asû prepared herbal remedies, bandages and plasters. The two often worked together.

questions.stem: Scribal schools of the Old Babylonian period continued to train students to copy texts in Sumerian. This shows that:
options: Sumerian was still the everyday spoken language of Hammurabi's Babylon
Akkadian had not yet been written down in cuneiform at that time
scribes were forbidden to write letters in any language but Sumerian
Sumerian remained a language of learning after it stopped being spoken
questions.explanation: Akkadian was the spoken and written language of daily business, but Sumerian survived as a classical language of religion and literature, like Latin in medieval Europe. Akkadian had been written in cuneiform since Sargon's time.

questions.stem: The gateways of Assyrian palaces at Kalhu and Nineveh were guarded by lamassu. These were:
options: bronze statues of the king standing in front of his chariot
painted mud-brick towers on which archers kept watch at night
carved stone lions that held the stele of the king's laws
huge stone figures of winged bulls or lions with human heads
questions.explanation: Lamassu were protective spirits carved as colossal human-headed winged bulls or lions, flanking palace doorways to ward off evil and impress visitors. Inside, walls were lined with carved relief slabs showing royal deeds.
